content:
Running a large construction project in ops is like steering a large ship through tight turns. A ship that size can't turn at the last minute, no matter how good the captain is. The decisions that matter get made long before the turn.

I spent the first half of my career obsessed with execution, first as an engineer, then as a project manager. My job was to fix the problem in front of me and get it done. I was good at it, and I was proud of it.

Then I became an executive and started managing projects from sales through closeout. For the first time, I could see the whole life of a project instead of just the part I was standing in. Something I'd been too close to notice became obvious.

By the time a project reaches ops, its outcome is largely decided not by how hard the team works but by what happened, or didn't happen, in preconstruction.

Here's the part that took me years to accept. Once construction starts, a project almost always gets worse, not better. Costs don't fall mid-project, scope doesn't shrink on its own, surprises show up, and each one eats into the plan. In ops, you can absolutely make a bad situation worse but beating what was planned is rare. Most of the time, the best ops can do is protect what preconstruction set up.

That's why so many great project teams still end up firefighting. They aren't failing at execution. They're inheriting a plan that was already stretched before day one.

It took me years of experience to understand that. It's also why Kanav Hasija and I built MeltPlan around preconstruction. We didn't want to build dashboards that executives react to and squint at after the damage is done. We wanted to help teams get the plan right while it can still be changed.

content:
How large GCs can expedite AI adoption ? 

First, let me say this: construction companies have gotten a lot better at adopting technology. Most large GCs now have dedicated innovation and technology groups. That's not nothing. That's a real shift from when I started in construction in 2008.

But there's still a gap that costs everyone time. I see it repeatedly from both sides of the table.

Here's the pattern: a startup approaches a large general contractor. The GC is interested. Things move forward until they hit the long, slow slog of IT security review, procurement, and internal approvals. Months pass. By the time a decision is made, the startup has burned runway. The GC has lost momentum. Neither side got what they needed.
What makes it worse is how most evaluations are structured.
I've seen two approaches:
Option 1: The GC lets the startup run their demo on the startup's own data. Convenient. Fast. Almost useless. Any decent startup has carefully curated a dataset that makes their product look great. You're not learning how the tool performs on your work. You're watching a highlight reel.
Option 2: The GC tests the product on their own data, but only after clearing IT, security, and legal. By then, you've invested months before knowing if the product actually works.

Having been on the both sides of the table. Here's what I think a win-win situation looks like:
Large GCs should build a small library of pre-anonymized evaluation datasets. A few drawing sets. Some estimates. A handful of QC logs and RFIs. Real data, scrubbed of anything sensitive. A "golden standard" for each one, meaning a human expert has already done the same workflow so you have a baseline to compare against.
When a startup comes to you, hand them the eval set first. See how their product performs on your problems vs human experts work! 
This does two things at once:
It gives your team an apples-to-apples comparison, not a vendor demo
It gives the startup a reality check with real feedback on how they hold up against actual construction data.
The startups worth working with will welcome this. The ones who push back probably shouldn't be in your pipeline!

From System of Record to System of Execution! 


Bessemer Venture Partners had a panel discussion around vertical AI.  I found the panel discussion between Shreesha Ramdas and Kanav Hasija very enlightening. Shreesha defined Pre-AI SaaS as a system of record and need for AI startups to become system of execution!

This statement was an epiphany for me. Traditionally, construction SaaS has been the digital clipboard. Frontline teams record field data, middle management polices it for quality, and executives squint at dashboards to find problems. It’s effective, but reactive. And Projects fail when this reporting chain breaks or slows down.

AI must move beyond being a system of record to become a system of execution! This requires AI to do more than capture data; it must significantly reduce man-hours or automate workflows like code compliance, drawing take-offs, or RFP responses. 

However, there is a dangerous trap: The Accuracy Gap. Speed without precision is just a faster way to fail. If an AI tool is faster but produces subpar results that a human has to spend hours correcting, you haven’t gained efficiency—you’ve just moved the bottleneck. 

Don’t switch to AI for the hype. Switch because it matches or exceeds expert human performance (which is a hard problem to solve for most workflows). Rigorous evaluations are the only way to bridge the gap between "faster" and "better".

I enjoyed my conversation with fellow cofounders at a venture west panel attended by large General Contractor decision makers. One of the key topics of discussion was: how do you sell to large GCs?

Before you think about the product, you have to understand the mindset.
In my experience, a project manager on a large construction job should be called project chaos manager. The job is to manage the imperfections of the real world in addition to the project issues. Schedules shift, material timelines can change, crews depend on decisions made in real time, and a single bad call can cascade into weeks of delay and additional costs!

My instinct as a PM was always to trust what is tried and tested especially when it came to technology. Not what's new!! 
That's the opposite of most startup cultures, where "move fast and break things" is almost a badge of honor.
In construction, you can lose your job for breaking things. Breaking things can lead to a missed milestone, a cost overrun, a safety risk.
So when a tech company walks into a GC's office pitching AI, the PM's first question isn't "what can this do?" It's: "Has this been tested? Will it hold up? What happens when it fails?"
Construction companies don't want to be guinea pigs. They want software that they know has been tested and can be relied on. Construction software is and needs to be held to a higher bar than any consumer app!
In my next post, I will explain what I see as a way to improve technology adoption for both GCs and technology vendors.

content:
The “open frontier” in LLMs is an illusion.

Not because open models are useless, but because there is no frontier there. What exists is a redistribution layer. Valuable, but not a frontier.

What’s actually happening?

The open ecosystem is downstream of the closed one, not by accident, but by design.

This is structured distillation: prompt the frontier model at industrial scale, harvest the reasoning and tool-use traces, and train on the outputs. The dataset is manufactured from the teacher.

• OpenAI alleged exactly this against DeepSeek.

• Anthropic documented it: DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax generated 16M+ exchanges with Claude through ~24,000 fraudulent accounts. When a new Claude model dropped mid-campaign, MiniMax redirected nearly half its traffic within 24 hours. You don’t pivot in 24 hours by accident. That’s an extraction pipeline tracking the frontier in real time.

• Dream inside a dream: (dedicated to Nolan:)) Thinking Machines’ Inkling, by its own admission, bootstrapped post-training on synthetic data from Kimi K2.5, on a DeepSeek-V3-mirroring architecture. A distillation of a distillation.

Why the ceiling exists?

A student trained on the teacher’s outputs is bounded by the teacher’s distribution. Distillation compresses capability; it never originates it. So open tracks closed with a lag, cheaper, smaller, but rarely ahead.

Rare bench exceptions do exist on record: Kimi K2.6 edging a frontier closed model on SWE-Bench Pro. But the devil is in the details.

So “open will surpass closed” is a pipe dream:

Every such claim describes a student outrunning its own textbook. It doesn’t happen unless open labs bring something genuinely original: novel learning paradigms, real sample efficiency, or self-generated signal. That’s the only door, and almost nobody is walking through it.

What’s actually worth watching?

The redistribution economy. Distilled intelligence at a fraction of the cost fits a wide band of real work: extraction, classification, and internal agents. The smart enterprise play is mix and match: route commodity tasks to cheap open weights, reserve the frontier for work that truly needs it. Meanwhile, the inference providers serving those weights are getting genuinely good, faster, cheaper, and climbing into agentic serving. That’s where open compounds.

Open isn’t inventing the frontier (at least not now). It’s industrializing it and racing the frontier’s price curve.

But can OpenAI’s recent 5.6 economics challenge this distribution game or not is to be seen in the coming days.

content:
Would you rather bet on a genius who sometimes goes astray, or a mediocrity guaranteed never to?

That is the design principle to think about frontier models.

It becomes a false choice once imagination and execution are separated.

Ramanujan brought Hardy extraordinary results, many unproved and some wrong. Hardy did not make him ordinary. He put rigor around the originality without extinguishing it.

Distillation can make a student outperform its teacher on a benchmark. It still does not make imitation a theory of discovery. When the teacher supplies both the answers and the boundary of acceptable thought, departures are penalized by design. A model forbidden to leave what its teacher already accepts is poorly designed to discover what its teacher missed.

Wrong candidates are the price of searching beyond known answers. Rogue actions are not.

The answer is neither lobotomy nor license. Let generation roam inside a sandbox; gate consequential action through verification. Contain the risk, not the imagination.

Breakthroughs do not come from eliminating deviation. They come from finding the deviation that turns out to be right.

Take your cue from your own life, art and history. Not from some company pushing narratives for securing their business model.

A model that never surprises you may be easier to trust. It is a poor bet to move the frontier.

content:
Two months ago, the White House signed an Executive Order to drive housing affordability. Today, the administration published a set of permitting best practices. We’re proud to have helped shape both.

Here are three changes that we are especially excited about:

1) Cumulative permit approval timelines, or “Shot Clocks”. Under 60 days for right-to-build approval. Under 30 days for construction permits and inspections.

For builders and contractors, predictable timelines mean projects can be scheduled, staffed, and financed with confidence. For municipalities, a defined service standard delivers clarity.

2) AI and technology for expedited permit approval. The federal government named artificial intelligence as a recommended tool for permitting modernization.

Permitting today involves outdated software, paper files, and teams that haven't grown alongside permit volumes. Repetitive application preparation, triage, and review is a sweet spot for AI. It automates the tedious, high-volume parts so teams can focus on the work that actually requires human judgment. That means faster turnaround, and higher-quality review for projects that need it.

3) No retroactive application of new or changed building codes after permit submission. The rules in effect when a permit is filed should be the rules that apply throughout the project. 

This one is common sense and benefits builders and municipalities equally. Builders get execution certainty: no mid-project rule changes. Municipalities get cleaner, faster reviews: when the code baseline is locked at permit submission, there's no ambiguity about which version applies, driving fewer correction cycles as a result.

At PermitFlow, we built our company on the belief that permitting works better when everyone in the process has clarity: builders know what's required, municipalities get what they expect, and the rules are consistent and transparent for both sides. These best practices point us in that direction.

content:
Hotels don’t fail because of tech.

They fail because they underestimate the human work around the tech.
Once Hotel am Konzerthaus Vienna - MGallery Collection  (208 rooms) decided to rebuild guest engagement, they weren’t chasing features. They were chasing three fragile human systems:
✅ Upsells (that guests actually say “yes” to)
✅ Unified communication (so no guest gets lost in the cracks)
✅ Staff adoption (so the tool doesn’t become shelfware)

Here’s what broke in the old status quo:
❌ Their previous upselling engine delivered—sometimes. But high commissions and inconsistent results meant it couldn’t scale.
❌ Communications were fragmented: email, SMS, phone, in‑person. Delays, dropped messages, confusion.
❌ Every time someone said “we’ll add one more system,” the staff sighed. Another login. More change. More friction.

So they picked Duve. But note: Duve never starred. The story is about how they used it.

Early in onboarding, Hotel Am Konzerthaus insisted on one dedicated contact. Less hand‑off, fewer dropped threads. That actually mattered. The team set up core flows in days—not weeks. Within three days they saw their first upsell. (Yes, real revenue.)

One December: ~€6,500 in upsell revenue from well-timed offers (pre‑arrival emails, bundled check‑in offers, mid‑stay app prompts).
 Guest satisfaction? A 4.7 in the internal Duve rating.

More importantly: the front desk staff weren’t drowning in extra work. They had relief. They had clarity.

This wasn’t about installing “another tool.” It was about rethinking who should do the upsell, who should do the messaging, and who should intervene (only when a guest really needed it).

📖 Lesson: The tool you pick is only as good as the design discipline you apply around it.

If your upsell logic, guest flows, or adoption process remain reactive and fragmented, the tool becomes just another burden. The real work is in turning your communications + offers into a coherent guest journey—so guests see value and staff see less noise.

If your team had to pick one workflow to consolidate right now—what would it be?

Yesterday, I wrote about why Vertical AI is a different business model than SaaS. CRE is the example that makes the thesis concrete.

Commercial real estate moves trillions of dollars. And it still runs on spreadsheets, faxes, and gut instinct.  No sector is more ripe for AI disruption. And no sector has resisted technology longer.

Here is why. The data layer does not exist. Leases are abstracted by paralegals. Due diligence arrives as unstructured PDFs. Underwriting models live in Excel files passed around with track changes. Documents are not structured. Information is not portable. Without a clean data layer, AI agents cannot act.
That is not a workflow problem. That is an architecture problem.

This is exactly the vertical AI thesis in practice. The incumbents -- CoStar, Yardi, MRI -- were built for a world where humans access data through interfaces. They were not built for a world where AI agents consume data through APIs and act autonomously. That architectural difference is not fixable with a product update.

Keyway.ai is building the data layer CRE never had. Automated lease abstraction. AI-native due diligence workflows. Underwriting models that update dynamically. Built for agents from day one.

Not a point solution bolted onto legacy software. A ground-up reimagination of how CRE gets done.

The disruption window is wide open. The incumbents are slow. The data moat compounds with every new lease, every new deal, every new asset under management.

Every major analyst firm has made the same prediction for 2026: agentic AI moves from experimentation into enterprise production. Autonomous agents with real tool access, real memory, and real decision-making authority — deployed at scale.

That shift changes the security threat model entirely. When an AI agent can send emails, execute code, query databases, and trigger financial transactions, a successful prompt injection attack is no longer a nuisance. It is a breach.

Indirect prompt injection is now ranked the number one threat in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and Generative AI 2025. It appears in 73% of production AI audits according to the same report. Microsoft has flagged it as one of the most widely used techniques in AI security vulnerabilities reported to them. And yet most teams are still trying to solve an architectural problem with probabilistic guardrails — asking one LLM to police another. That is not a defense. That is theater.

The root cause is structural: LLMs concatenate trusted instructions and untrusted data in the same context window. Until you separate control flow from data flow at the system level, you are patching the wrong layer.

This is exactly what the CaMeL Framework addresses. CaMeL (Capability-based Multi-LLM System) is the first architectural defense that structurally prevents untrusted data from ever influencing program control decisions — using a privileged LLM to generate workflow logic and a quarantined LLM to handle untrusted inputs, with a custom interpreter enforcing capability policies in real-time.

AI security failures aren’t theoretical anymore. Here are 3 numbers that should stick with you:
 - 80%+ of all phishing emails between Sept 2024 and Feb 2025 used AI to some extent
 - $410 million in deepfake-related fraud losses in just the first half of 2025 alone
 - 35% of real-world AI security incidents were caused by simple prompts - no code required

We’re shipping agents into production at record speed, and most of us are barely thinking about what happens when someone decides to break them.

This is why implementing these 3 practices is now table-stakes:
1. Guardrails in your prompts: cheap, fast, minimum viable. Do this always.
2. Red teaming before you ship: use the lab, run PyRIT, get a report, fix gaps.
3. Architectural thinking for high-stakes apps: look at CaMeL if your agent touches real data or real tools.

Security isn’t something you bolt on after launch. By the time you find out your agent is broken, someone else already knew.

Ilya said the quiet part out loud on Dwarkesh's pod, but most people still aren't processing what it means.

Here's what's actually happening inside AI labs. 

Research teams have entire divisions that do nothing but create new RL training environments specifically designed to boost benchmark scores. They treat AIME, SWE-bench, and MMLU like standardized tests. The model practices 10,000 hours on competitive programming problems until every proof technique is at its fingertips.

Then it fails to fix a simple bug in production without introducing two new ones.

Sutskever used the perfect analogy. Student A grinds 10,000 hours of competitive programming. Memorizes every algorithm, every edge case, every proof technique. Becomes the #1 ranked competitive coder in the world. Student B practices 100 hours but has "it." Intuition. Taste. The ability to learn new things quickly.

Who has the better career? Student B. Current AI models are all Student A.

The benchmark gaming runs deeper than most realize. Studies have shown data contamination inflates model scores by 20-80% on popular benchmarks. The training-test boundary is porous. Models memorize answers rather than learn concepts. And when you control for contamination, much of what looks like intelligence is pattern-matching on seen data.

This explains the economic puzzle Ilya pointed to. Models score 100% on AIME 2025. They hit 70%+ on GDPval beating human professionals. Yet businesses still struggle to extract value. The benchmark performance says genius. The P&L says otherwise.

The sample efficiency gap tells you everything. A human teenager learns to drive any car after 10 hours. An AI model might need millions of examples and still fail on slight variations. A human learns a concept once and applies it everywhere. Models need to see the exact pattern thousands of times and still choke when the formatting changes slightly.

Sutskever's diagnosis: we're moving from the "age of scaling" (2020-2025) back to the "age of research." The belief that 100x more compute would transform everything is dying. His $3B company SSI is betting that the next breakthrough comes from solving generalization, not stacking more GPUs.

The labs know this. 

That's why the benchmark arms race is accelerating. 

It's easier to show impressive numbers than admit the fundamental approach might be plateauing.

The world is talking about single founder billion dollar companies but not talking(or not even whispering)  about solo cyber attackers that now can cause billions dollars harm. Here is one,  

A Russian-speaking, actor with limited technical skills used AI tools (including DeepSeek and Anthropic Claude) to compromise over 600 FortiGate firewall devices across 55 countries between January and February 2026. 

This means as we all get efficient with AI tools ( claude code) 
•	these tools has lowered the barrier to entry for cybercrime: a single low-skill operator ran simultaneous the intrusions will be common if not already. 
•	BTW, the entire attack succeeded through basic security hygiene failures: exposed management ports and weak, single-factor credentials.
•	Why is that possible now- attacker used AI as a force multiplier, achieving operational scale that would have previously required a significantly larger and more skilled team.

How it happened ?

The attacker scanned the internet for FortiGate management interfaces  attempted to log in using commonly reused or default credentials. Once inside the FortiGate appliance, the attacker extracted full device configurations revealing AD(active directory) credentials, network topology, and connected systems.

And then, AI took over 
• ARXON MCP server-  all scan results and stolen configurations were automatically fed into the MCP server, which maintained a growing knowledge base for each target.
• DeepSeek generates attack plans - the attacker used DeepSeek to analyze data and generate tactical attack plans for each victim network.
• Claude Code conducts live vulnerability assessment -  Anthropic's Claude coding agent was configured to produce vulnerability assessments during active intrusions and execute offensive tools on victim systems.
• And a custom Go-based tool called CHECKER2 automated parallel VPN scanning and target processing.

This resulted in full domain compromise, backup infrastructure targeted and put physical access control at risk that persisted across multiple countries. 

Complete domain compromise means the attacker can read every email, access every file, and potentially deploy ransomware that encrypts everything with no backup to restore from. 

Here is a PM checklist not fancy but needed specially in the AI age.
- Ensure perimeter devices and all internal software are up to date.
- Enforce MFA everywhere, rotate credentials, eliminate default passwords.
- Isolate management interfaces, backup servers, and sensitive systems.
-  Deploy detection for post-exploitation indicators including DCSync, NTLM relay, and unauthorized account creation.
- Implement immutable, air-gapped backups that cannot be destroyed by a compromised domain admin.
- Update threat models to account for AI-augmented attackers operating at greater speed and scale.

What actually makes a great AI Product Manager?
Last time I shared that I'm mentoring MAHESH YADAV and Keyuri Anand's AI PM cohort on Maven. But what does an AI PM do?

Think of it this way:
*Traditional PMs are chess players: mastering fixed rules
*AI PMs are poker players: making optimal decisions under uncertainty, with incomplete information, where the rules evolve. They frame AI problems, identify risks, and guide teams toward feasible solutions.

Here are the 5 pillars I believe make great AI PMs:
1️⃣ Strategic Problem Framing
Not every nail needs an AI hammer. The best AI PMs ruthlessly prioritize where AI creates disproportionate value, assessing data readiness, and ensuring regulatory compliance. They recognize AI limitations, potential biases, and implications of misuse or security risks.
Ask yourself:
→ Is the data unstructured, does the problem require complex decision-making, are there evolving rule sets?

2️⃣ Technical Proficiency
Know what goes into building and evaluating AI models:
Agent Architecture: Break complex AI systems into composable sub-agents. Think: user intent classifier → context retriever → response generator → safety filter, not one giant black box.
MVP Scoping: Identify minimum capabilities that prove value.
Evaluation Frameworks: Demos that work for 10 use cases are easy. Scaling to 1,000+ cases requires systematic evaluation. Start with manual rubrics, then scale with LLM-as-judge patterns.

3️⃣ Responsible AI & Compliance
In 2025, "move fast and break things" doesn't fly with AI. Regulators are watching. Users are skeptical.
Your job:
→ Build guardrails into your architecture for safety and reliablility
→ Ensure transparency: Can users understand why AI made a decision?
→ Ensure fairness: Are you testing across diverse user segments?
→ Navigate compliance: EU AI Act, state-level regulations, industry rules

4️⃣ AI-Native Business Models
Pricing AI products is fundamentally different from SaaS. Models get cheaper. Expectations rise. Competitors move fast.
Key questions:
→ What's your free tier strategy? (Acquisition vs. qualification)
→ What drives conversion? (Time saved? Quality? Capabilities unlocked?)
→ How do you grow week-over-week? (Usage depth vs. user breadth)
→ What happens when GPT-5 cuts your costs by 10x?
The best AI PMs design pricing strategy resilient to rapid capability and cost changes.

5️⃣ Domain Expertise
By 2026, every company will have AI features.
The differentiator is knowing:
 → Where to apply AI within a specific domain
 → Why it creates ROI for that specific workflow
 → How to integrate it into existing processes without disruption
Generic AI expertise is table stakes. Domain expertise is the moat.

The Bottom Line:
AI PMs sit at the intersection of technical possibility and commercial viability.

Not maliciously. Just inevitably. There's no system to hold it, no process to extract the lessons, and the next project starts from scratch.

The approach is straightforward: start documenting project data in a way that AI can read and learn from. Not just storing files, but structuring the information so patterns emerge across projects.

Which scopes consistently run over? Which site conditions created the most change orders? Where did the estimate diverge from reality, and why?

A GC that builds this over three to five years of projects has something genuinely valuable: institutional memory that doesn't walk out the door when a senior PM retires.

Most of the conversation about AI in construction is about reading drawings faster or automating takeoff. That's real. But the bigger, quieter opportunity is learning from what already happened.

content:
Two things I keep hearing from construction teams right now.
"AI is going to take our jobs." and "AI is doing a shitty job."

Neither is wrong. But they can't both be right about the same thing.
What's happening is simpler than it looks. Most people are treating AI as one monolithic capability. It isn't. Breaking it into three capability buckets changes how you think about all of it:

Language | Vision | Reasoning

Language AI is genuinely good, near 90% on frontier benchmarks. Summarizing documents, pulling clauses from specs, writing reports. If a task is language-based, automate it. The value is proven.

Vision is in the useful-but-verify zone. Reading drawings, matching takeoff quantities, nearly zero in 2024, around 50% now. High enough to help. Not high enough to trust without proper evaluations and benchmarks.

Reasoning is early. Scope gap analysis, constructability calls, the calls a senior estimator builds over 20 years. The curve is steep, but we're at the beginning of it. Test it. Don't automate with it yet.

Once you see AI through this lens, both things become true. Just about different capabilities.

Construction people scared about jobs are watching Language models work. They're right to pay attention. Construction firms frustrated that AI got the takeoff wrong? Also legitimate, because Vision and Reasoning are still early, and most teams aren't running the right benchmarks before deploying.

For any AI use case your team is evaluating, the first question isn't "does AI work?" It's which of the three buckets does this task fall into.

That one question changes everything about how you pilot, evaluate, and decide.
